parent: III. Clarifying the Gates of Dhyāna-Pāramitā

zh: 第三、料簡通、別二門。問曰：若爾者，何故如前分別？答曰：一切義理，有通有別，教門對緣，益物不同，異說無咎。復次，前非了義之說，未可定執。問曰：三門互得通者，今就事中數息而學，得證九想、八背捨、自性等禪不？答曰：或得或不得。初學者不得，二乘學自在定者得，菩薩具足方便波羅蜜者，隨意無礙。
en: Third, resolving points of doubt about the gates taken together and taken separately. Question: If this is so, why were they distinguished separately before? Answer: In every matter of doctrine, there is both a general and a specific way of taking it; the gate of teaching, matched to the occasion, benefits beings differently — there is no fault in giving differing accounts. Furthermore, what was said before is not a statement of fully complete meaning, and should not be clung to as fixed.

Question: If the three gates interpenetrate one another, then if a practitioner, in actual practice, learns by counting the breath, can this bring realization of the nine contemplations, the eight liberations, the dhyāna of self-nature, and the like? Answer: it may or may not. A beginner cannot; one of the two lesser vehicles who has mastered sovereign concentration can; a bodhisattva complete in the pāramitā of skillful means can move among them freely, without hindrance.

zh: 問曰：何故云初學不得？有人數息發九想、背捨，念佛慈心，此復云何？答曰：此發宿緣不正，因修得證，緣盡則滅謝不進，終不成就次第法門。至下內方便中明善根發相，當廣分別。餘二門類然可知。
en: Question: Why is it said that a beginner cannot? Yet there are those who, counting the breath, give rise to the nine contemplations, the liberations, or a mind of buddha-recollection and loving-kindness — how, then, is this to be understood? Answer: This is the arising of conditions from past lives; it is not realization properly attained through cultivation — once those conditions are exhausted, it fades away and does not advance further, and in the end does not accomplish the sequential dharma-gates. This will be explained fully further below, in the inner expedient means, where the marks of wholesome roots arising are clarified. The remaining two gates may be understood by the same kind of reasoning.

zh: 釋禪波羅蜜次第法門卷第一之上
en: End of Fascicle One, Upper Part, of the Shi Chan Boluomi Cidi Famen.

A useful closing caution: interpenetration between the gates is not automatic or guaranteed just because a practitioner happens to experience something from a "further" gate while working in a "nearer" one. Zhiyi's example — someone counting the breath who suddenly experiences the nine contemplations or a feeling of buddha-recollection — is explained away as a leftover condition from a past life, not a sign of readiness, and warns that it fades without producing real, sequential progress. This closes topic 3, and with it, the whole of fascicle 1's upper half.

zh:
釋禪波羅蜜次第法門卷第一之下
隋天台智者大師說
弟子法慎記
弟子灌頂再治
en:
Explaining the Sequential Dharma-Gates of Dhyāna-Pāramitā, Fascicle One, Lower Part
Spoken by the Great Master Zhiyi of Tiantai, of the Sui dynasty
Recorded by his disciple Fashen
Revised and edited by his disciple Guanding

items.zh: 正明諸禪次第 · 有漏法
parent: IV. Distinguishing the Sequence in Which Dhyāna-Pāramitā Is Explained

zh: 行者既知禪門之相，菩薩從初發心乃至佛果，修習禪定，從淺至深，次第階級，是義應知。今略取經論教意，撰於次第，故《大品經》云：「菩薩摩訶薩次第行，次第學，次第道。」辨禪定次第，即為二意：一者、正明諸禪次第；二者、簡非次第。
en: The practitioner, having now understood the mark of the gates of dhyāna, should also understand this: that from a bodhisattva's very first arising of the mind through to buddhahood, the cultivation of dhyāna-concentration proceeds from the shallow to the deep, through graduated stages and sequence. Here, in brief, the intent of the sūtras and treatises is drawn together to compile this sequence — hence the Larger Sūtra says: "The bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices in sequence, studies in sequence, and walks the path in sequence." Distinguishing the sequence of dhyāna-concentration has two parts: first, rightly clarifying the sequence of the various dhyānas; second, distinguishing what is not sequential.

zh: 一、正釋諸禪次第義者，行人從初持戒清淨，厭患欲界，繫念修習阿那波那，入欲界定，依欲界定，得未到地，如是依未到地，次第獲得初禪乃至四禪，是名內色界定。次為大功德緣外眾生，受樂歡喜，次第獲得四無量心，是名外色界定。此八種禪定雖緣內外境，入定有殊，而皆屬色界攝。行者於第四禪中厭患色如牢獄，滅前內、外二種色，一心緣空，得度色難，獲得四空處定，是名無色界定。此十二門禪皆是有漏法。
en: First, rightly explaining the meaning of the sequence of the various dhyānas: the practitioner, beginning from pure moral discipline, grows weary of the desire realm, fixes the mind in mindfulness, and cultivates ānāpāna, entering the concentration of the desire realm. In dependence on the concentration of the desire realm, the "not-yet-arrived" state is attained; and in dependence on that, the first dhyāna is attained in sequence, on up through the fourth dhyāna — this is called the inward concentration of the form realm. Next, for the sake of great merit, taking external sentient beings as the object, receiving joy and delight, the four immeasurable minds are attained in sequence — this is called the outward concentration of the form realm. These eight kinds of concentration, though they take inward or outward objects and differ in how concentration is entered, all belong to the form realm.

The practitioner, within the fourth dhyāna, grows weary of form as though it were a prison, extinguishes the two prior kinds of form, inward and outward, and, with a single mind, takes emptiness as the object; having thus crossed over the difficulty of form, the concentration of the four formless bases is attained — this is called the concentration of the formless realm. These twelve gates of dhyāna are all contaminated dharmas.

This is the treatise's first full run through the classical Abhidharma map of concentration: the four dhyānas of the form realm (inward, through breath-practice) plus the four immeasurable minds (outward, toward other beings) make eight "form realm" attainments, and the four formless bases beyond them make twelve in total — the "twelve gates of dhyāna." All twelve are still called "contaminated" (有漏, sāsrava) because none of them, on their own, cut through the delusion that produces further rebirth; that requires the uncontaminated dhyānas introduced next.

zh: 次此應明亦有漏亦無漏禪。行者既得根本禪已，為欲除此禪中見著，次還從欲界修六妙門。所以者何？此六門中，數、隨、止是入定方便，觀、還、淨是慧方便，定愛慧策。愛故說有漏，策故說無漏。此六法多是欲界、未到地、四禪中具足，亦有至上無色地者。次此應明十六特勝，橫則對四念處，竪則從欲界乃至非想，但地地中立觀破析故，能生無漏。次應說通明觀，前十六特勝總觀故麁，今通明別觀故細。此禪亦從欲界至非想，乃至入滅定。此三種禪亦名淨禪，五種禪中猶是根本攝。
en: Next, what is both contaminated and uncontaminated dhyāna should be clarified. Once the practitioner has attained the root dhyānas, in order to remove the views and attachments found within them, one returns again, from the desire realm, to cultivate the six wondrous gates. Why is this? Among these six gates, counting, following, and stilling are the expedient means for entering concentration; contemplating, returning, and purifying are the expedient means of wisdom. Concentration is what is craved, wisdom is what spurs one onward — because it is craved, it is called "contaminated"; because it spurs one on, it is called "uncontaminated." These six practices are, for the most part, complete within the desire realm, the "not-yet-arrived" state, and the four dhyānas, though some extend up to the formless bases as well.

Next, the sixteen special excellences should be clarified: taken across, they correspond to the four foundations of mindfulness; taken down through the stages, they run from the desire realm all the way to the peak of existence — but because contemplation is established and analysis carried out stage by stage, they are able to give rise to the uncontaminated. Next, the thorough-and-bright contemplation should be explained: the sixteen special excellences just given contemplate as a whole, and so are coarse; the thorough-and-bright contemplation contemplates each part separately, and so is fine. This dhyāna, too, runs from the desire realm all the way to the peak of existence, up through entering the concentration of cessation. These three kinds of dhyāna are also called "pure dhyānas," and, among the five kinds of dhyāna, still belong to the category of the root attainments.

The six wondrous gates (六妙門) — counting, following, stilling, contemplating, returning, and purifying the breath — get their name "wondrous" from exactly this dual character: the first three build concentration (and so are still "craved," still contaminated), the last three build wisdom (and so "spur one onward" toward the uncontaminated). This is Zhiyi's own subject in a separate, shorter treatise, the Six Dharma Gates to the Sublime, already published in English translation by Bhikshu Dharmamitra — see this fascicle's translation notes for why this project translates independently of that edition.

items.zh: 無漏禪次第 · 行行次第
parent: IV. Distinguishing the Sequence in Which Dhyāna-Pāramitā Is Explained

zh: 今明無漏禪次第之相，即有二意不同：一者、行行次第；二者、慧行次第。行行次第，所謂觀、鍊、熏、修。初明觀禪次第，有六種禪：初修九想，無漏之前，用此對治，破欲界煩惱故。次八念，為除修九想時怖畏心生故。次十想，壞法人於欲界修此十想，斷三界煩惱故。次八背捨，不壞法人修此觀禪，對治三界根本定中見著故。次明八勝處，為於諸禪定觀緣中得自在故。次明十一切處，為欲廣禪定中色心令普遍故。乃至修六神通，由是觀禪攝。
en: Now, as for the mark of the sequence of uncontaminated dhyāna, there are two distinct aspects: first, the sequence of practice-conduct; second, the sequence of wisdom-conduct. The sequence of practice-conduct is what is called observing, refining, perfuming, and mastering.

First, clarifying the sequence of observing dhyāna: there are six kinds of dhyāna here. First, the nine contemplations are cultivated — prior to the uncontaminated, these serve as the antidote, breaking the afflictions of the desire realm. Next, the eight recollections, to remove the fear that arises while cultivating the nine contemplations. Next, the ten contemplations — practitioners of the "destructible-dharma" type cultivate these ten contemplations within the desire realm, severing the afflictions of the three realms. Next, the eight liberations — practitioners of the "indestructible-dharma" type cultivate this observing dhyāna, as an antidote to the views and attachments found within the root concentrations of the three realms. Next, the eight stations of mastery are clarified, for the sake of gaining mastery over the objects observed within the various concentrations. Next, the ten totality-bases are clarified, in order to make form and mind pervasive throughout concentration. And on up through the cultivation of the six supernormal powers — all of these belong to observing dhyāna.

zh: 次明鍊禪者，即九次第定為總，前定觀二種禪，令心調柔，入諸禪時，心心次第無間故，及有覺有觀等三三昧皆是鍊禪攝。次明熏禪。熏禪者，即是師子奮迅三昧，順逆次第入出熏諸禪，令定觀分明純熟，增益功德故。次明修禪。修禪者，即是超越三昧，於諸禪中超越入出，為得無礙自在解脫故。
en: Next, clarifying refining dhyāna: the nine sequential concentrations serve as its overall name — the two prior kinds of dhyāna, concentration and observation, make the mind pliant and gentle, so that, when entering each dhyāna in turn, one mind-moment follows the next without any interval. The three samādhis — the samādhi possessing initial thought and sustained reflection, and the rest — also belong to refining dhyāna.

Next, clarifying perfuming dhyāna. Perfuming dhyāna is precisely the lion's-sport samādhi: entering and emerging from each dhyāna in turn, in forward and reverse sequence, perfuming every dhyāna in turn, so that concentration and observation both become clear and fully ripened, and merit is increased.

Next, clarifying mastering dhyāna. Mastering dhyāna is precisely the transcendence samādhi: transcending, entering, and emerging among the various dhyānas, in order to attain unobstructed, self-mastered liberation.

zh: 是以《大品經》云：「菩薩摩訶薩住般若波羅蜜，取禪波羅蜜。除諸佛三昧，入餘一切三昧，若聲聞三昧，若辟支佛三昧，若菩薩三昧，皆行皆入。」餘一切三昧者，根本定是。若聲聞三昧者，三十七品、空、無相等三三昧，四諦十六行是。若辟支佛三昧者，十二因緣三昧是。菩薩三昧者，自性禪等，皆名三昧是。菩薩住諸三昧，逆順出入八背捨，依八背捨逆順出入九次第定，依九次第定逆順出入師子奮迅三昧，依師子奮迅三昧逆順出入超越三昧。是菩薩依諸三昧，得諸法相等，齊此始是二乘行，行共禪滿。何以故？大阿羅漢亦得超越三昧故。
en: Hence the Larger Sūtra says: "The bodhisattva-mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of wisdom, takes up dhyāna-pāramitā. Setting aside the buddhas' own samādhis, they enter every other samādhi — whether the śrāvaka's samādhi, the pratyekabuddha's samādhi, or the bodhisattva's samādhi — practicing and entering all of them alike." "Every other samādhi" refers to the root concentrations. The "śrāvaka's samādhi" refers to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the three samādhis — emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness — and the sixteen aspects of the four truths. The "pratyekabuddha's samādhi" refers to the samādhi on the twelve links of dependent origination. The "bodhisattva's samādhi" refers to the dhyāna of self-nature and the like — all of these are called samādhi.

The bodhisattva, abiding in these various samādhis, enters and emerges from the eight liberations in forward and reverse order; in dependence on the eight liberations, enters and emerges from the nine sequential concentrations in forward and reverse order; in dependence on the nine sequential concentrations, enters and emerges from the lion's-sport samādhi in forward and reverse order; and in dependence on the lion's-sport samādhi, enters and emerges from the transcendence samādhi in forward and reverse order. It is by depending on these various samādhis that the bodhisattva attains the characteristics of all dharmas, and so on. Only this far does the practice of the two lesser vehicles reach: here the shared dhyāna of practice-conduct is complete. Why is this? Because even the great arhat can also attain the transcendence samādhi.

"Observing, refining, perfuming, mastering" (觀鍊熏修) names four successive grades of working with dhyāna once concentration is already established — not four different objects of meditation, but four different things one does with the whole set of attainments. Observing dhyāna is the largest category: as the text itself says, it has six kinds of dhyāna — the nine contemplations, the eight recollections, the ten contemplations, the eight liberations, the eight stations of mastery, and the ten totality-bases — on up through the six supernormal powers. Refining, perfuming, and mastering then each take the entire stock of prior attainments and put it through a further process — smoothing the mind's movement between states (refining), cycling through them repeatedly to deepen mastery (perfuming), and finally leaping freely between them in any order (mastering, the transcendence samādhi). The passage's closing point is worth sitting with: everything up through the transcendence samādhi is still shared with the two lesser vehicles — "even the great arhat can also attain" it. What comes next belongs to the bodhisattva alone.

quiz.q: Can one who learns by counting the breath realize the nine contemplations, the eight liberations, the samādhi of self-nature, and the like?
options: only beginners can
always
it may or may not: a beginner cannot; a two-vehicle practitioner who has mastered sovereign concentration can; a bodhisattva complete in skillful means moves freely
never
quiz.why: "It may or may not. A beginner cannot; one of the two lesser vehicles who has mastered sovereign concentration can; a bodhisattva complete in the pāramitā of skillful means can move among them freely, without hindrance." Interpenetration depends on the practitioner's level.

quiz.q: Some people counting the breath suddenly give rise to the nine contemplations, the liberations, or buddha-recollection and loving-kindness. How does the text view this?
options: it arises from a past-life condition; once that is exhausted it fades and does not advance, never accomplishing the sequential dharma-gates
it shows one can skip the sequence and go straight to the bodhisattva's dhyāna
it is a demonic state and meditation must stop at once
it shows the noble fruit has been attained
quiz.why: "Once that root-condition is exhausted, it fades away and does not advance further, and in the end does not accomplish the sequential dharma-gates. This will be explained fully further below, in the inner expedient means." It is neither a noble fruit nor called demonic; the point is that it does not lead to steady progress.

quiz.q: If the gates interpenetrate, why were they assigned separately before?
options: the later account is wrong; the earlier one stands
the earlier account was a mistake to be corrected
every doctrine has general and specific aspects, teaching suits the occasion, so differing accounts are no fault; the earlier statement was not of complete meaning
the two accounts contradict and cannot be reconciled
quiz.why: "In every matter of doctrine, there is both a general and a specific way of taking it; the gate of teaching, matched to the occasion, benefits beings differently — there is no fault in giving differing accounts. Furthermore, what was said before is not a statement of fully complete meaning, and should not be clung to as fixed."

quiz.q: What makes up the "twelve gates of dhyāna"?
options: the six wondrous gates plus the six powers
the nine contemplations plus the three samādhis
the four dhyānas (inward form-realm), the four immeasurables (outward form-realm), and the four formless bases
the eight liberations plus the four immeasurables
quiz.why: The four dhyānas are "the inward concentration of the form realm," the four immeasurables "the outward concentration of the form realm," and the four formless bases "the concentration of the formless realm. These twelve gates of dhyāna are all contaminated dharmas."

quiz.q: Why are the four immeasurable minds called the "outward concentration of the form realm"?
options: because non-Buddhists also practice them
for the sake of great merit they take external sentient beings as their object
because they belong to the formless realm
because they are practiced outside the body
quiz.why: "Next, for the sake of great merit, taking external sentient beings as the object, receiving joy and delight, the four immeasurable minds are attained in sequence — this is called the outward concentration of the form realm." Both inward and outward kinds "all belong to the form realm."

quiz.q: How does the practitioner pass from the fourth dhyāna into the formless bases?
options: visualizing the Buddha's image
growing weary of form as of a prison, extinguishing inward and outward form, and taking emptiness as the object with a single mind
cultivating the immeasurables toward external beings
counting the breath to ten thousand
quiz.why: "The practitioner, within the fourth dhyāna, grows weary of form as though it were a prison, extinguishes the two prior kinds of form, inward and outward, and, with a single mind, takes emptiness as the object." Taking external beings as object is the immeasurables, still in the form realm.

quiz.q: Having attained the root dhyānas, why does the practitioner return to the desire realm to cultivate the six wondrous gates?
options: because the root dhyānas have been lost
to remove the views and attachments found within those dhyānas
because the six gates are shallower and must be practiced again from the start
to be born in the desire heavens
quiz.why: "Once the practitioner has attained the root dhyānas, in order to remove the views and attachments found within them, one returns again, from the desire realm, to cultivate the six wondrous gates." The root dhyānas are contaminated and breed attachment; the six gates contain the expedient means of wisdom that counters it.

quiz.q: Among the six wondrous gates, which three are the expedient means of wisdom?
options: contemplating, returning, purifying
following, stilling, returning
counting, following, stilling
counting, contemplating, purifying
quiz.why: "Counting, following, and stilling are the expedient means for entering concentration; contemplating, returning, and purifying are the expedient means of wisdom."

quiz.q: Why does the text call the six wondrous gates "both contaminated and uncontaminated"?
options: concentration is craved and wisdom spurs one on — craved, hence contaminated; spurring, hence uncontaminated
half is in the desire realm and half in the form realm
because it is practiced only in the formless realm
ordinary people practice it contaminated, sages uncontaminated
quiz.why: "Concentration is what is craved, wisdom is what spurs one onward — because it is craved, it is called 'contaminated'; because it spurs one on, it is called 'uncontaminated.'" The six are mostly complete within the desire realm, the not-yet-arrived state, and the four dhyānas, not only the formless.

quiz.q: How does the text distinguish the sixteen special excellences from the thorough-and-bright contemplation?
options: the reverse
the two are identical
the sixteen excellences contemplate as a whole and so are coarse; thorough-and-bright contemplates each part separately and so is fine
the excellences are uncontaminated, thorough-and-bright contaminated
quiz.why: "The sixteen special excellences just given contemplate as a whole, and so are coarse; the thorough-and-bright contemplation contemplates each part separately, and so is fine." Both, with the six gates, are "both contaminated and uncontaminated," also called pure dhyānas.

quiz.q: In the sequence "observing, refining, perfuming, mastering," what is perfuming dhyāna?
options: the nine sequential concentrations: one mind-moment following the next without interval
the nine contemplations: countering desire-realm afflictions
the lion's-sport samādhi: entering and emerging from each dhyāna in forward and reverse order
the transcendence samādhi: leaping among the dhyānas
quiz.why: "Perfuming dhyāna is precisely the lion's-sport samādhi: entering and emerging from each dhyāna in turn, in forward and reverse sequence, perfuming every dhyāna in turn." Refining is the nine sequential concentrations, mastering the transcendence samādhi, and the nine contemplations belong to observing.

quiz.q: In the sequence of observing dhyāna, why are the eight recollections cultivated right after the nine contemplations?
options: to gain mastery over the objects observed in concentration
to make form and mind pervasive in concentration
to sever the afflictions of the three realms
to remove the fear that arises while cultivating the nine contemplations
quiz.why: "Next, the eight recollections, to remove the fear that arises while cultivating the nine contemplations." Severing three-realm afflictions is the ten contemplations, mastery over objects the eight stations, and pervasiveness the ten totality-bases.

quiz.q: According to the text, which kind of practitioner cultivates the ten contemplations, and which the eight liberations?
options: only bodhisattvas cultivate either
the reverse
ordinary people cultivate both
the "destructible-dharma" type cultivates the ten contemplations; the "indestructible-dharma" type the eight liberations
quiz.why: "Next, the ten contemplations — practitioners of the 'destructible-dharma' type cultivate these ten contemplations within the desire realm ... Next, the eight liberations — practitioners of the 'indestructible-dharma' type cultivate this observing dhyāna."

quiz.q: Why does the practice-conduct sequence, even up to the transcendence samādhi, remain dhyāna "held in common"?
options: because buddhas do not cultivate it
because even the great arhat can attain the transcendence samādhi
because ordinary people can attain it too
because the transcendence samādhi is contaminated
quiz.why: "Only up to this point does the practice of the two lesser vehicles coincide with the bodhisattva's own, dhyāna held fully in common between them. Why is this? Because even the great arhat can also attain the transcendence samādhi." What follows, the nine unshared dhyānas, belongs to the bodhisattva alone.
